guide.title: Workforce Safety & Wellness
guide.lead: You can't help anyone if you become a patient. Read every scene before you walk in, park to protect yourself on roads, wait for police when violence is possible, and look after your body and mind over a long career.

sections.title: Safe to enter?
sections.question: Violence or weapons, traffic, fire, hazardous materials, unstable structures, animals – or a situation you can't read?
sections.yes: Stay back. Stage out of sight and out of range, call police, fire or hazmat, and enter only when it's safe or with a police escort into a protected (warm) zone.
sections.no: Enter, keep scanning, keep an exit behind you, and stay with your partner.

steps.title: Block
steps.text: Park upstream at an angle so the vehicle shields the work area.

steps.title: Be seen
steps.text: High-visibility vests on everyone; warning lights on; cones or flares upstream.

steps.title: Watch traffic
steps.text: Never turn your back to traffic; load from the protected side.

steps.title: Belt up
steps.text: Seat belts in the patient compartment whenever care allows: vehicle incidents are the leading cause of on-duty EMS deaths.

steps.title: Identify from a distance
steps.text: Placards, labels, shipping papers, binoculars; look it up in the Emergency Response Guidebook.

steps.title: Treat after decontamination
steps.text: Patients come to you in the cold zone.

sections.title: Three kinds of stress
rows: Fight or flight during or right after a call: racing heart, shaking, tunnel vision
Breathe, take a break, talk with a peer; it usually settles
Flashbacks, nightmares, avoidance weeks later (possible PTSD)
Exhaustion, cynicism, less empathy, feeling ineffective, drinking more
Act early: rest, support, professional help

sections.title: After a critical incident
items: Psychological first aid: safety, calm, connection, practical help
Peer support and watchful waiting: most reactions settle within weeks
Routine single-session debriefing (CISD) is no longer recommended; any session should be voluntary
Symptoms beyond 1 month, or getting worse: get professional help
Thoughts of suicide: tell someone today

sections.title: Everyday wellness
items: Sleep and fatigue management between shifts
Real meals and water on shift; not energy drinks
Strength and flexibility training for lifting
Time off, family and life outside EMS

quiz.q: Gradual burnout over months or years of EMS work is:

quiz.explanation: A set of support services after critical incidents.

quiz.q: First action when you suspect hazardous materials:
options: Isolate the area and deny entry
Put on a hazmat suit and enter
quiz.explanation: Stay upwind, uphill, upstream; call hazmat.

quiz.q: Current guidance on routine single-session debriefing (CISD) after a critical incident:
options: Not recommended routinely; offer psychological first aid, peer support and follow-up
quiz.explanation: Traditionally held 24–72 hours after; WHO and NICE now advise against routine debriefing.

quiz.q: Which is NOT a sign of cumulative stress?
The leading cause of on-duty EMS deaths is:
options: Vehicle incidents: ambulance crashes and being struck by traffic
quiz.explanation: Belts, safe driving and roadway protection save lives.

quiz.q: Best ambulance position at a roadway incident:
options: Upstream, as a barrier between traffic and the scene
Behind the scene with lights only
Lights off to avoid distracting drivers

quiz.q: After 8 years in EMS a provider feels numb, dreads work, snaps at family and drinks more after shifts. Most likely?
quiz.explanation: Act early: rest, support, professional help.

quiz.q: After a traumatic pediatric arrest, what support helps most?
options: Psychological first aid and peer support now, with follow-up and referral if symptoms persist
quiz.explanation: Watchful waiting with support; help if symptoms last beyond 1 month.

options: Pack healthy meals and snacks; stay hydrated
One big meal at the end

quiz.q: Fight-or-flight during a critical call is:
quiz.explanation: It usually settles after the call.

quiz.q: Active shooter at a school; police still searching. You should:
options: Stage safely until police declare it safe or escort you into a protected zone
Wait in the ambulance with the doors open
Put on a vest and go in alone
quiz.explanation: Rescue task forces enter only with police protection.

flashcards.question: Three types of stress
flashcards.answer: Acute (during or right after a call), delayed (weeks later; possible PTSD), cumulative (burnout from long exposure).

flashcards.question: CISM
flashcards.answer: Critical Incident Stress Management: support after critical incidents. Today the focus is psychological first aid, peer support and follow-up rather than routine debriefing.

flashcards.question: Defusing vs debriefing
flashcards.answer: Defusing: short and informal, within hours. Debriefing (CISD): structured, traditionally 24–72 hours later – no longer recommended routinely; voluntary only.

flashcards.question: Leading cause of on-duty EMS deaths
flashcards.answer: Vehicle incidents: ambulance crashes and being struck by traffic.

flashcards.question: Signs of burnout
flashcards.answer: Emotional exhaustion, cynicism, less empathy (compassion fatigue), feeling ineffective, more alcohol.

flashcards.question: Suspected hazardous materials
flashcards.answer: Upwind, uphill, upstream; identify from a distance; isolate and deny entry; call hazmat; treat after decontamination.

flashcards.question: Domains of wellness
flashcards.answer: Physical (sleep, food, fitness), emotional and mental – all linked.

flashcards.question: When to get help after a bad call
flashcards.answer: Symptoms lasting beyond 1 month, getting worse, or affecting work and home – or any thoughts of suicide.

critical.scenario: 2 a.m., 'person down' in a dark alley; caller hung up. Several people stand in the shadows at the far end. Police are 8 minutes away. Your partner wants to go in.
critical.question: Best decision?

options.t: Stage at a safe distance and wait for police to secure the scene

options.f: An unknown group in the dark is a threat.

critical.explanation: Scene safety comes before patient care.
critical.kpi: Recognizes scene hazards and stages until secure

critical.scenario: End of a 14-hour shift: a 3-year-old drowning didn't survive. Your partner, whose child is the same age, says 'I'm fine, I'll have a beer and forget it' – hands shaking, voice unsteady.
critical.question: Best action?

options.t: Stay with them, offer peer support now and the employee support service, and check in over the next days
Report them as unfit for duty

critical.explanation: Watchful waiting with support; refer if symptoms persist beyond 1 month.
critical.kpi: Supports a colleague after a critical incident

critical.scenario: Dusk, two-lane highway, traffic passing at speed. Car into a tree, smoke from the engine. The driver has a deformed femur and difficulty breathing; no police or fire yet.
critical.question: Most critical safety step besides care?

options.t: Park to block the lane, high-visibility vests on, cones out, request fire
Pull him out because of the smoke
options.f: Smoke alone isn't fire; assess and get fire service.

critical.explanation: If fire develops, an emergency move is justified.
